code.text: MRI of the brain without contrast, with susceptibility-weighted imaging: mild generalized atrophy, slightly more in the frontal lobes, with hippocampi in the normal range for age (medial temporal atrophy score 1 on each side); a small area of old injury (encephalomalacia with hemosiderin) at the tip of the right frontal lobe; seven microbleeds at the gray-white junction of both frontal lobes; a few small white matter hyperintensities (Fazekas 1); a cavum septi pellucidi; no infarct, mass, subdural collection or hydrocephalus

Neuropsychological testing, about three hours with breaks: slowed processing speed and reduced attention, set-shifting and verbal fluency; learning and free recall reduced but much better with cues and recognition (a retrieval pattern rather than rapid forgetting); naming, language and visual perception intact; consistent with mild cognitive impairment of frontal-subcortical type; effort measures valid; mood and PTSD symptoms noted as contributors

Cognitive processing therapy for PTSD with the clinic psychologist: twelve weekly sessions, adapted for memory problems (shorter sessions, written one-page summaries, phone reminders, and his care partner helping with practice between sessions, with his consent)
Advance care planning conversation, about 30 minutes, with him and his care partner; his capacity to name a health care agent and state his values was assessed and present
Physical therapy for balance and strength: ten sessions with a home exercise program (sit-to-stand, heel raises, tandem stance, walking program)

text.div:
SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD

  • Cognitive work-up under the Alzheimer's Association guideline: history from him and his care partner, MoCA, function, depression and PTSD screening, first-tier blood tests (blood count, metabolic panel, B12, TSH), a medicine review for anticholinergic and sedating drugs, a sleep apnea screen, hearing and vision checks, and brain MRI
  • Cognitive neurology consultation at the memory clinic to stage the impairment, weigh traumatic brain injury, traumatic encephalopathy syndrome, Alzheimer's disease, vascular disease and the effects of PTSD and depression, and choose further testing
  • PTSD treatment by shared decision: cognitive processing therapy with the clinic psychologist, weekly for about twelve sessions, adapted for memory problems; and sertraline 25 mg each morning, raised to 50 mg after four to six weeks if tolerated, with sodium checked two weeks after starting and after the increase; benzodiazepines avoided
  • Collaborative safety plan with warning signs, coping steps, people to call, the clinic number and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; medicines kept by his care partner; PHQ-9 item 9 and safety reviewed at every visit
  • Falls: STEADI assessment, physical therapy for balance and strength with a home program, and a home safety check
  • Measurement-based care: PCL-5 and PHQ-9 at each chronic-care visit during treatment; MoCA yearly or sooner with change; medicine review every visit
  • After the diagnosis: no cholinesterase inhibitor or memantine, which are not shown to help mild cognitive impairment or traumatic brain injury; memory strategies (one calendar, phone reminders, a fixed daily routine), exercise, social activity, sleep and blood pressure care; repeat neuropsychological testing in twelve to eighteen months or sooner with change; Alzheimer's disease biomarker testing explained and declined for now, as it would not change his care
  • Travel and money safety: carry a card with his address and his care partner's number, share his phone location, travel with company on unfamiliar routes, and set up shared oversight of bills
  • Caregiver support: education about mild cognitive impairment and PTSD, the Alzheimer's Association 24/7 Helpline (which serves all causes of cognitive impairment), a caregiver class and a burden check; the Medicare GUIDE model explained for if dementia develops later
  • Advance care planning while he can take part fully: a health care agent, his values and goals of care, at the annual wellness visit

resource.title: Emile Griffith synthetic care plan
resource.description: A neurocognitive disorder after repetitive head impacts and a later assault, with chronic PTSD, in a 67-year-old retired world champion boxer who comes with his care partner because of memory loss and confusion. The episode follows the 2024 Alzheimer's Association DETeCD-ADRD guideline (history from him and an informant, the MoCA and CDR, function, reversible causes, a medicine review, brain MRI and neuropsychological testing, disclosure and counseling) and shows how the NINDS 2021 criteria for traumatic encephalopathy syndrome are research criteria, not a clinical diagnosis; how PTSD, depression and moral injury (guilt and self-blame after a fight in which his opponent died) are screened and treated under the VA/DoD 2023 PTSD guideline, with cognitive processing therapy adapted for memory problems, sertraline with sodium checks, and a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; why no cholinesterase inhibitor is used for mild cognitive impairment; falls; caregiver support; and advance care planning while he can take part fully. It respects the way he described his own life and sexuality, and makes no claim about his private health beyond the public record.
